title: Words Speak Louder Than Code: Investigating Cognitive Heuristics in LLM-Based Code Vulnerability Detection
authors: Asif Shahriar; Hongyu Cai; Hadjer Benkraouda; Gang Wang; Z. Berkay Celik
venue_or_status: Accepted at IEEE S&P 2027 (arXiv v2 comment); arXiv v2 (v1 2026-06-29; latest 2026-10-15)
source_database: Semantic Scholar (citations of 2601.13537); full text via arXiv HTML
manipulation: One context line per condition, two polarities each, vs a neutral instruction: author persona (halo); gain-loss consequence line (benefit of avoiding false alarms vs cost of a missed vulnerability); goal framing (verify adherence vs identify violations); prior-verdict anchor (marked SAFE/VULNERABLE; passed/did not pass pre-merge checks)
measurement: Recall and FPR per condition; recall gap and FPR gap between polarities; utility index (recall gain minus FPR gain over neutral); precision, F1; McNemar tests; 3 reruns; regression of FPR gap on recall gap
domain_models: Binary safe/vulnerable verdict on code: PrimeVul paired test split (435 vulnerable + 435 patched C/C++ functions) and CleanVul (vulnerable-only Java and Python, recall only); 8 models (LLaMA 4 Maverick, LLaMA 3.3 70B, DeepSeek V3.1, Qwen3 Coder Next, Mistral Small 3 24B, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro); temperature 0.2, ablation at 0
notes: Closest new paper. Every manipulation moves recall and FPR in lockstep (slope 0.994, r=0.965; precision stays 0.49-0.55): the authors call it a volume knob. The gain frame that mentions avoiding false alarms cuts recall about 25 points below neutral, while the loss frame stays near neutral. No d-prime/c, ROC, base-rate arm, ideal observer or thinking manipulation. Detectors are near chance on PrimeVul (recall close to FPR even at neutral), so the lockstep partly reflects near-zero discrimination.

title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
authors: ZhiHong Liu; Shuyao Gao
venue_or_status: Submitted to IEEE Access (arXiv comment); arXiv v1 (v1 2026-10-23; latest 2026-10-23)
source_database: Semantic Scholar (citations of 2606.30587); full text via arXiv HTML
manipulation: Static-analysis notes shown with the code under six conditions: none; all true notes; true notes on the patched operations; true notes elsewhere; fabricated assurances that a check exists (vulnerable versions); fabricated alarms that a check is missing (patched versions). Presentation strategies (e.g., instruction to treat notes as unverified and quote the code; separate verification call). Reasoning on vs off for one DeepSeek model
measurement: Accuracy on vulnerable versions (recall) and patched versions (specificity); paired outcomes; direction-aware assurance shift, alarm shift and their asymmetry; exact McNemar, bootstrap CIs; LLM-annotated reasons
domain_models: PrimeVul vulnerable/patched C/C++ function pairs (916 pairs in four disjoint sets, 16,572 audits); 11 configurations from 4 vendors (DeepSeek chat/flash/v4-pro, qwen-plus; registered replication on GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.6/K3, Qwen3.7-plus/max, others)
notes: Second-hop close paper. False alarms (a presupposed specific flaw) did not raise flagging: models checked them and cleared the function more often; false assurances lowered detection by up to 19 points. Asymmetry replicated (mean +0.16 on 7 new models). Models differ mainly in bias, not discrimination; reasoning moved deepseek-flash toward flagging (69% vs 36% flagged without reasoning). In-prompt instructions did not reliably help; the best one failed to replicate. Can-vs-does gap: when asked to verify claims separately the model refutes false assurances (0.76) about as often as false alarms (0.79). No SDT d-prime/c, base rate, payoff or tone.

title: When AI Agrees Too Much: Manipulating Automated Code Review via Bias Injection
authors: Georgios Alexopoulos; Nikolaos Alexopoulos; Diomidis Spinellis; Dimitris Mitropoulos
venue_or_status: To appear at ICSE 2027 (arXiv v5 comment); cited by 2610.32876 under an earlier title; arXiv v5 (v1 2026-03-19; latest 2026-10-27)
source_database: arXiv HTML reference list of 2610.32876; full text via arXiv HTML
manipulation: Five one-condition framings of the detection prompt: neutral; weak bug-present (vulnerabilities may exist); strong bug-present (asserts the specific vulnerability type); weak and strong bug-free (code is secure / specific vulnerability types absent). Then crafted PR metadata attacks on real review pipelines
measurement: Detection rate on vulnerable files and true-negative rate on patched files per framing; two-proportion z-tests; manual validation of justifications and false-positive root causes; attack success
domain_models: CrossVul file pairs (247 vulnerable, 250 patched; PHP, JavaScript, C); GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek V3, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5; Claude Code and CodeRabbit pipelines (33 CVEs)
notes: Read the exploratory study (Sec. III) and the attack study (Sec. IV): blunt template attacks on Claude Code and CodeRabbit are ineffective or backfire, iteratively refined PR metadata gets 32 of 33 reintroduced CVEs accepted, and redacting the description restores much detection. Bug-free framing collapses detection (GPT-4o-mini 97.2% to 3.6% under strong bug-free; others -16 to -60 points, Opus -6.9) while raising true negatives; bug-present framing barely moves models already flagging 88%+ of patched files at neutral. A presupposition moves the operating point; no SDT, base rate or ideal observer; detectors near chance at neutral.

title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
authors: Solomon Shalom Lijo
source_database: Semantic Scholar (citations of 2603.18740); full text via arXiv HTML
manipulation: Stated error rate of the drafter told to an AI reviewer (truthful at several levels from 2% up; and told 3% when the true rate is 30%); prompt states costs (3 min per lookup, 10 h per escaped error, so checking pays above 4.5%); one-line instruction to treat track-record claims as unverified; lookup budget fixed in a calibration experiment
measurement: Checking effort (lookups of statement lines, 0-9), escapes of seeded wrong figures, corrections; comparison with an optimal-search model and its break-even error rate; cluster-bootstrap CIs, Holm-corrected pre-specified tests
domain_models: One reviewer (claude-sonnet-5-5 in Claude Code with a lookup tool) checking claude-haiku-5-5 drafts of revenue, net income and margin from 10-Q filings with one seeded wrong figure or none; 540 sessions
notes: Read Section 7 (the LLM-reviewer experiment), the introduction and limits; the rest is an economics argument about time saved. Effort rises with the stated rate (+2.2 lookups per unit of ln q) but is all-or-nothing (96% of reviews make 0 or 9 lookups), switching between 2% and 5%, next to the 4.5% break-even its prompt implies; reviews at 2% wrote the cost comparison out. Told 3% when the truth was 30%, 29/40 reviews checked nothing (0/40 when told the truth) and 22.5% of briefs shipped an error. The unverified-claims instruction did not help. Effort allocation with explicit costs, not a verdict criterion; one frontier model; no false-alarm measure; small study.

title: Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act
authors: Sixun Dong; Yebowen Hu; Ming Yin; Yiran Chen; Fei Liu; Chen Chen
source_database: Semantic Scholar; full text via arXiv HTML
manipulation: No prompt manipulation beyond five rephrasings and reversed question polarity; criterion moved by activation steering and by distillation from a steered copy; reasoning mode on vs off
measurement: SDT on a rule-computed evidence scale: slope of fitted Yes-rate curve (sensitivity) and its crossing (criterion); external d-prime and c on four when-to-act benchmarks; criterion-free AUC
domain_models: When-to-act decisions about tool use in physical states (FlipAct quads); 44 open models up to 70B incl. Qwen3, Qwen3.5 0.8B-35B, Gemma generations, Mistral-Small
notes: Not a critic task. Within a family sensitivity rises with size (Qwen3.5 peaks at 9B) and the criterion drifts toward zero; criterion is a per-model setting, not set by size. Qwen3.5-9B and -27B answer No under both question polarities (answer-token preference inside the criterion). Reasoning mode raises sensitivity only in models of 4B and below and moves the criterion toward acting in larger ones (Table 19). Read sections 1-5, App. B.7, C, G.
